findings.headline: Homelessness is 50% above the England average and driving capital and revenue investment with ongoing demand uncertainty
findings.detail: Section 13 (benchmarking) shows 'In 2025/26 Q1, DLUHC assessed the number of households as homeless per thousand in Milton Keynes was 2.77, which was greater than All English unitary authorities' average number of households assessed as homeless per thousand of 1.84.' The council has invested in accommodation, and while section 9.21 states 'no additional pressures have been put in the MTFP' because it is 'being well managed,' the high baseline and continued population growth create ongoing volatility.
findings.matters: Homelessness 50% above national average indicates a structural demand challenge in the council's area (driven by housing affordability and population growth) that may require sustained above-average investment.
findings.figures: 2.77 households assessed as homeless per 1,000 vs England average of 1.84 (2025/26 Q1); 863 households in temporary accommodation vs England average of 316
findings.quote: In 2025/26 Q1, DLUHC assessed the number of households as homeless per thousand in Milton Keynes was 2.77, which was greater than All English unitary authorities' average number of households assessed as homeless per thousand of 1.84.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) waste funding is declining and uncertain beyond 2026/27
findings.detail: Section 6.4 states 'The funding level beyond 2026/27 is not clear as this will be dependent upon actual EPR collected by the government, behaviour changes by the sector and how government may choose to allocate funding to authorities.' The council has assumed £4.819m in 2026/27 but table 4 shows it declining to £4.219m (2027/28), £3.519m (2028/29), £2.819m (2029/30). This is a new grant introduced in the Autumn Budget 2024 with no clarity on multi-year funding.
findings.matters: A declining and uncertain income stream (£2m reduction over three years) from a brand-new source means the council cannot assume it as permanent baseline funding and will need to find alternative savings.
findings.figures: £4.819m 2026/27, declining to £2.819m by 2029/30 (total MTFP decline of £2.0m)
findings.quote: The funding level beyond 2026/27 is not clear as this will be dependent upon actual EPR collected by the government, behaviour changes by the sector and how government may choose to allocate funding to authorities.

findings.headline: Business Rates Retention Scheme entirely reset in 2026/27, removing all business growth income and introducing valuation appeal risk
findings.detail: Section 8.3 states 'the Business Rates Retention Scheme (BRRS) has been entirely reset in 2026/27, starting on April 1, 2026. All business rates growth has been removed and redistributed using new funding formulas from that date.' Section 8.7 identifies significant collection risks: 'Ratepayers are able to raise challenges to their rating valuations and where successful the rateable value is reduced... we have assumed in the 2026/27 budget that appeals losses will result in the loss of 1.5% of the net rates payable.' The council expects to collect net rates of £249.185m but retains only £67.701m baseline.
findings.matters: Removal of all business growth income and a 1.5% loss assumption on valuation appeals (with scope for 'significant variations') means the retained business rates income is now entirely baseline and more volatile, without the benefit of economic growth in Milton Keynes (which has strong GVA growth of £16.7bn).
findings.figures: Net rates collected £249.185m; council retains £67.701m baseline (50% of net rates less fire authority share and tariff/levy); 1.5% appeal loss assumption
findings.quote: the Business Rates Retention Scheme (BRRS) has been entirely reset in 2026/27... All business rates growth has been removed and redistributed using new funding formulas from that date.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes waste recovery contract is being re-procured mid-cycle with current operating costs of £5.9m pressure in 2026/27
findings.detail: Section 9.23 states 'The Council is currently re-procuring the contract to operate and maintain the MKWRP. The new contract anticipated start date is Oct 2026. Whilst the commissioning is still ongoing, current operating costs have been used as the basis of the pressure of £5.9m in 2026/27. The new contract will include incentives for the provider to reduce this cost pressure and when savings are confirmed, they will be incorporated into future MTFP workings.' This is a major commercial contract with uncertain outcomes.
findings.matters: A £5.9m cost pressure from a waste contract re-procurement with savings incentives 'to be confirmed' means the full year impact is contingent on commercial negotiation outcomes, introducing upside/downside risk to the baseline.
findings.figures: £5.9m contractual change pressure in 2026/27 (section 9.23); section 10.3 identifies £6.762m total savings/income 2026/27-2029/30
findings.quote: The Council is currently re-procuring the contract to operate and maintain the MKWRP. The new contract anticipated start date is Oct 2026... current operating costs have been used as the basis of the pressure of £5.9m in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Agora regeneration scheme costs and revenues remain unquantified and a Cabinet decision is pending
findings.detail: Section 4.3 notes that the MTFP 'includes the costs of interest and minimum revenue provision relating to the financing of the Agora project within the capital programme. No assumptions have yet been included in the MTFP for the income anticipated from this scheme. This will be updated once build costs are more certain and decisions are finalised on how this asset will be held.' Section 1.19 records 'The regeneration of the former Agora shopping centre and the adjoining car park has been a Council priority for over two decades' and that 'a separate Cabinet Decision is planned to be taken on 3 February 2026 to further update on this regeneration, as well as set out future decision making to deliver it.'
findings.matters: A major capital scheme with decades of difficulty, unresolved build costs, and unmodelled income makes the council's financial projections incomplete. Any increase in borrowing costs or delay in income crystallisation will worsen the MTFP gap.
findings.figures: Agora interest and MRP costs embedded in capital financing costs (£1.692m total over MTFP) but income from the scheme not yet assumed
findings.quote: The reported gap includes the costs of interest and minimum revenue provision relating to the financing of the Agora project within the capital programme. No assumptions have yet been included in the MTFP for the income anticipated from this scheme. This will be updated once build costs are more certain and decisions are finalised on how this asset will be held.

findings.headline: Contractual inflation in social care has spiked 28% in one year and now projects £37.593m pressure over the MTFP
findings.detail: Section 9.9 states 'Contractual Inflation for 2026/27 has risen by £2.202m since February 2025... Over the medium term it is estimated that contractual inflation will rise to a budget pressure of £37.593m, an increase of 28% from February 2025, which is a significant risk to the Councils financial position.' The main driver is National Living Wage inflation (section 9.10): the Foundation Living Wage is forecast to increase 5.58% for 2026/27, then 3.54% in 2027/28. Adult services alone carry £5.802m of contractual inflation in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A 28% year-on-year increase in contractual inflation projections (driven by care worker wages) is well ahead of core inflation and signals that care placement costs and staffing costs are accelerating, likely exceeding the council's savings and income plans.
findings.figures: £2.202m increase since February 2025; £37.593m total MTFP pressure (28% increase from prior forecast); £5.802m adult services inflation in 2026/27; 5.58% Foundation Living Wage increase 2026/27
findings.quote: Contractual Inflation for 2026/27 has risen by £2.202m since February 2025... Over the medium term it is estimated that contractual inflation will rise to a budget pressure of £37.593m, an increase of 28% from February 2025, which is a significant risk to the Councils financial position.

findings.headline: Looked after children have surged 26% in three years with uncertain peak and £17.125m pressure built in
findings.detail: Section 9.16 records LAC numbers rising 'from an average of 379 in 2023/24 to 477 in 2024/25 (26% increase)' and in December 2025 standing at 481. Section 9.18 explicitly states 'There remains a lot of uncertainty in the MTFP regarding the longer-term forecasts for Children's Placements. Of the £17.615m budget pressure in the medium term, £7.639m has been built into the 26/27 budget. This is because future demands at this point are difficult to predict.' The service believes the peak has been reached but acknowledges uncertainty and risk to budget projections.
findings.matters: A 26% surge in the most expensive placements (high-cost residential care) with acknowledged forecasting uncertainty means actual outturn could significantly exceed budget if the peak has not been reached or if placement numbers plateau at elevated levels.
findings.figures: LAC increased from 379 (2023/24) to 477 (2024/25) to 481 (December 2025); £17.125m MTFP pressure (£7.639m in 2026/27); additional staff costs £0.140m
findings.quote: Looked after Children (LAC) numbers over the last 3 years from an average of 379 in 2023/24 to 477 in 2024/25 (26% increase)... There remains a lot of uncertainty in the MTFP regarding the longer-term forecasts for Children's Placements... there is still some uncertainty and therefore a risk to the budget projection included in the MTFP.

findings.headline: High Needs Block (special education) will have zero reserves by March 2027 with no in-year contingency
findings.detail: Section 11.3 states the surplus will reduce from £3.103m to £1.173m in 2025/26 due to demand and inflation, and then 'the HNB 2026/27 budget has been balanced by using all of this remaining surplus. There will therefore be no surplus by the end of March 2027 and there is no contingency in year to allow for any volatility.' The statutory override protecting councils with deficits expires March 2027 (extended to end 2027/28), creating a cliff edge. Nationally, 2 in 3 councils carry HNB deficits forecast to reach £5bn by March 2026.
findings.matters: A zero-contingency ring-fenced budget block with a track record of overspend (currently in-year overspend in 2025/26) is a immediate budget risk that will force the general fund to absorb any overspend once the statutory override expires.
findings.figures: Surplus reduces from £3.103m budgeted to £1.173m forecast in 2025/26; used entirely in 2026/27 leaving £0m; £4.023m high needs block allocation increase for 2026/27 but insufficient to cover demand
findings.quote: the HNB 2026/27 budget has been balanced by using all of this remaining surplus. There will therefore be no surplus by the end of March 2027 and there is no contingency in year to allow for any volatility.

findings.headline: The council has a £14.139m cumulative funding gap across the MTFP period with no identified solution
findings.detail: The budget is balanced in 2026/27 but the gap grows to £1.632m in 2027/28, £6.927m cumulatively by 2028/29, reaching £14.139m by 2029/30. The council has put in place a 'Change Because We Have To' programme but no specific savings are attached to these future years. Section 10.5 states the council 'will need to take further difficult decisions' but these have not been identified.
findings.matters: A £14m unfunded gap over three years signals the council cannot deliver a balanced budget without major service reductions or further borrowing, which directly affects financial sustainability and borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £14.139m cumulative gap (£0m, £1.632m, £6.927m cumulative, £14.139m by 2029/30)
findings.quote: Looking beyond 2026/27, the funding gap is currently £14.139m. The Council will need to take further difficult decisions to address these challenges over this period.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Strategic Risk Register Aug 2025
findings.headline: Placement costs for children in care are rising, with no cap on demand.
findings.detail: Risk SR15 flags 'Increased costs due to failure to properly plan to ensure sufficient access to high quality placements' and lists as a trigger 'Change in demand for children (e.g. increase in LAC numbers, child protection referrals)'. The risk score is 15 (target 10), with no recent improvement. The council is attempting to grow in-house foster carer recruitment and adoption services, but the triggers suggest external market forces and demand are outpacing supply.
findings.matters: Placement costs (especially residential and external foster care) are a volatile line item that grows with demand and market prices. A council unable to forecast or limit this spend faces in-year budget pressure.
findings.figures: Current risk score 15, target 10. No specific cost figures disclosed.
findings.quote: Increased costs due to failure to properly plan to ensure sufficient access to high quality placements

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Strategic Risk Register Aug 2025
findings.headline: Milton Keynes has aging assets of similar vintage requiring more maintenance spend than budgeted.
findings.detail: Risk SR16 identifies that 'the assets are of a similar age which can lead to large numbers of defects/interventions being required. this leads to insufficient budget or budget exceeded for works required to appropriately maintain the assets.' This means the council faces a cohort risk: many assets reaching end-of-life at once, creating uneven demand spikes that current budgets cannot absorb.
findings.matters: A council with assets of similar age faces unpredictable lumpy maintenance demands and may need to borrow or defer maintenance. This is a precursor to service deterioration or unexpected capital pressure.
findings.figures: No specific budget figures disclosed, but the risk is identified as recurring and structural.
findings.quote: the age and quality of MK assets – the assets are of a similar age which can lead to large numbers of defects/interventions being required. this leads to insufficient budget or budget exceeded for works required to appropriately maintain the assets.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Strategic Risk Register Aug 2025
findings.headline: Housing landlord acknowledges insufficient budget for repairs due to rent cost cap and inflation.
findings.detail: Risk SR04 identifies the core problem: 'insufficient budget to deliver works to standard required, including external factors such as imposed rent cost cap, inflation and interest rates.' The risk is currently scored 9 (target 6), meaning it remains elevated. The council is taking action (condition surveys due 01/11/2025, NEC procurement by 01/04/2026) but acknowledges the gap between what it needs to spend and what it can spend.
findings.matters: Housing Revenue Account is a material asset and income stream. A council unable to maintain its housing stock to standard faces compliance failures, tenant claims, and regulator intervention. The rent cap + inflation squeeze is a known structural problem.
findings.figures: Current risk score 9, target score 6. Risk score higher than target indicates mitigation is incomplete.
findings.quote: Budget – insufficient budget to deliver works to standard required, including external factors such as imposed rent cost cap, inflation and interest rates.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Strategic Risk Register Aug 2025
findings.headline: Waste Recovery Plant carries up to £6.5M exposure from a single unplanned outage.
findings.detail: Risk SR13 details exposure from the Waste Recovery Plant's poor availability. The council is liable for up to £500k property damage plus up to 90 days of direct losses (less first 5 days) if the plant fails. The catastrophic boiler failure in October 2022 left the facility unavailable for 4 months and cost the contractors £2M per month, so maximum exposure could reach £6.5M. The plant has a history of only 60% availability. The council has now discovered a £4M annual cost delta in the income/expenditure model, equivalent to a gate fee of £60 per tonne.
findings.matters: The plant is critical waste infrastructure with severe financial consequences if it fails. The discovery of a £4M annual cost gap in the operating model suggests the council may have mispriced this service for years.
findings.figures: Maximum exposure £6.5M from a single failure; £500k property damage + 90 days direct losses; catastrophic boiler failure in Oct 2022 cost contractors £2M per month; new cost model reveals £4M annual delta; monthly cost approximately £840k (staff £300k pa, disposal £7.8M pa, insurances £1.1M pa, NNDR £800k pa).
findings.quote: The contractors losses owing to the catastrophic boiler failure equated to around £2M per month (including lost revenue, haulage and disposal and staff costs) so maximum exposure could be around £6.5M.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Strategic Risk Register Aug 2025
findings.headline: The council faces unprecedented savings requirements and exceptional financial challenges.
findings.detail: Risk SR07 explicitly identifies 'Exceptional Financial Challenges requiring unprecedented savings' as a trigger and consequence. This language signals the council believes it faces budget pressures beyond the norm, with triggers including failure to manage large increases in demand and failure to put in place business continuity plans for service provider failure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council has identified the scale of its own challenge. This language—'unprecedented'—suggests the finance team believes standard solutions are insufficient.
findings.figures: No specific savings target or amount disclosed, but categorised as 'unprecedented'.
findings.quote: Exceptional Financial Challenges requiring unprecedented savings
